title: Orsen and the Ledger
premise: When archivist Freya Dunmore receives a confession letter postmarked the day after a parishioner's funeral, she realizes the cathedral's locked crypt holds more than bones—it holds proof that a man everyone mourned was murdered, and that the witness who saw it all is officially recorded as dead. Following the ledger's falsified entries through seven years of town records, Freya uncovers a conspiracy of quiet complicity in which nearly every respected family played a part. The witness turns out to be the town's beloved doctor, living under a borrowed identity he took to survive the night of the murder. In the end, Freya must choose between filing the truth away like everything else and burning her own carefully constructed invisibility to testify before the statute expires.
about_author: Edmund Coldharbour is the pen name of a former parish records clerk who spent a decade cataloguing small-town archives across northern England. He writes mysteries about paper trails, buried secrets, and the people paid to keep both tidy.

chapters.title: Postmark
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Three days after old Tom Wicker's funeral, a confession letter arrives addressed to the crypt's dead—postmarked the day after the burial. Freya, who prides herself on order, hides it in an unfiled drawer instead of reporting it. Emotional beat: the first crack in her armor of routine, and the reader's first hint that her invisibility is a choice with costs.

chapters.title: The Locked Crypt
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She breaks protocol and enters the sealed crypt, finding Wicker's coffin already disturbed—and a second name scratched into the ledger: Ruth Calloway, deceased 2018, yet no death certificate exists. Emotional beat: dread mixed with a thrilling sense of purpose; for once, the archive is asking something of her rather than the reverse.

chapters.title: Everyone Loved Him
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Constable Idris Vane, who warns Freya off when she asks about Wicker's death certificate. The town's grief is genuine and uniform—too uniform, Freya notes. Emotional beat: isolation deepening as she realizes questioning the dead man means suspecting the whole living town.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Small Lies
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Cross-referencing parish ledgers, she finds a pattern: dates altered, tithes redirected, a fire report missing from 2018—the year Ruth Calloway 'died.' Emotional beat: the intoxication of discovery curdling into fear as she understands the falsifications were deliberate and protected.

chapters.title: The Doctor's Hands
chapters.summary: Dr. Elias Marsh's POV, revealed only at chapter's end. He treats a cut on Freya's hand and asks one question too many about the archive. Emotional beat: warmth laced with wrongness; readers sense kindness that knows too much, while Freya feels seen for the first time in years—and hates it.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She tracks Ruth Calloway to a burned cottage outside town and finds a hidden strongbox: photographs proving Wicker ran a blackmail operation funded by the parish council. Emotional beat: righteous anger giving way to vertigo—if everyone was a victim of Wicker, everyone had a motive.

chapters.title: Statute of Limitations
chapters.summary: Idris Vane's POV. The constable confesses privately that he falsified the death record under pressure from the council, believing he was protecting the town from scandal. He gives Freya until the statute expires in nine days. Emotional beat: reluctant alliance; two keepers of secrets deciding, together, to stop keeping this one.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Is Dead
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Following the ledger's final anomaly—a prescription refill signed in Ruth's handwriting last spring—she confronts Dr. Marsh. He admits he is Ruth's brother, living under a false identity since witnessing Wicker kill their father in 2018. Emotional beat: devastating recognition; the witness she hunted has been stitching her wounds all along.

chapters.title: Nine Days
chapters.summary: Marsh's POV. The council, tipped off by Vane's indiscretion, moves to seal the crypt permanently with Marsh inside the frame—accidents happen in old buildings. Freya races to extract him and the strongbox evidence. Emotional beat: breathless climax; the invisible woman becomes the most visible person in town, torch in hand at the crypt door.

chapters.title: Filed Under F
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, epilogue-style. Marsh testifies; the council falls; the statute closes over lesser crimes but not the murder. Freya files the true ledger openly in the archive, then adds her own name to the staff register for the first time—not the archivist, just Freya Dunmore. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; belonging earned not by hiding, but by being counted.
